title: Barley straw as an inhibitor of algal growth I: studies in the Chesterfield Canal
authors: Welch IM, Barrett PRF, Gibson MT, Ridge I
result: Per Semantic Scholar summary, rotting barley straw reduced filamentous algae in the canal and 'shows promise as a long-term method of controlling algae'. No numbers seen.
env_effects: Not reported in the summary seen.

title: The use of barley-straw to control general and blue-green algal growth in a Derbyshire reservoir
result: Per the project's snowball notes (from an abstract summary), phytoplankton productivity and cyanobacterial dominance were both significantly reduced without nutrient removal. Numbers not seen by this collector.
env_effects: Reported 'no short term deleterious environmental impact' in receiving streams; more grazers present.

title: An Assessment of the Effectiveness of Straw as an Algal Inhibitor in an Upland Scottish Loch
authors: Harriman R, Adamson E, Shelton R, Moffett G
organism: Algal blooms driven by a black-headed gull colony
scale: Upland loch, central Scotland; moored bales
dose: Moored barley straw bales (dose not in abstract)
result: Release of the inhibitory substance began 6-10 months after bale placement and lasted at least 18 months; cell numbers of the main species were affected but algal diversity was not.
env_effects: Bales became substrate/shelter and detritus trap for benthic invertebrates.

title: Limited Effects of Barley Straw on Algae and Zooplankton in a Midwestern Pond
scale: Replicated limnocorrals inside a 1 ha Iowa pond
result: No consistent algal growth inhibition for either filamentous or planktonic algae, and zooplankton community structure was unaffected. Authors attribute failure to low oxygen inside decomposing straw in stagnant ponds.
env_effects: No effect on zooplankton community structure.

title: The effects of barley straw (Hordeum vulgare) on the growth of freshwater algae
authors: Ferrier MD, Butler BR, Terlizzi DE, Lacouture RV
organism: 12 freshwater algae incl. Microcystis aeruginosa, Anabaena flos-aquae, Synura, Oscillatoria
scale: Lab bioassays of 12 unialgal cultures (nutrient media vs unfiltered or sterile-filtered barley straw liquor, replicate cultures) plus 6 central-Maryland ponds (0.2-1.6 ha, 1.8-4.3 m deep): 4 randomly assigned to straw, 2 untreated controls
dose: Ponds: 112 kg straw/ha in loosened, netted bales near the surface; lab: barley straw liquor
duration: Lab: two-week incubations; ponds: 21 May to 10 September 1998, sampled biweekly
result: Straw liquor significantly inhibited Microcystis aeruginosa, Dinobryon and Synura petersenii (Synura undetectable after two weeks) but stimulated Selenastrum, Spirogyra, Oscillatoria and Navicula. In ponds, biomass declined in both treated and control ponds after application and did not differ significantly between them on any date.
key_details: Lab: two-week bioassays with replicate cultures; initial Chl a was not measured, so algistatic vs algicidal action could not be separated except for Synura (disappeared). Anabaena flos-aquae, Chlorella, Ulothrix, Synedra and Scenedesmus were not significantly affected. Field: four treated (112 kg/ha) vs two control ponds in 1998, Chl a from pooled samples biweekly. Variation among ponds was very large (coefficients of variation 36-157% treated, 33-141% control), so the field test had low power; biomass fell in all ponds right after the first sampling.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record lists Anabaena flos-aquae among target species without noting it was unaffected; field dose (112 kg/ha) and low statistical power (4 treated vs 2 control ponds, CVs up to 157%) were missing. Spirogyra was stimulated by unfiltered liquor but inhibited by sterile-filtered liquor.

title: A series of experiments aimed at clarifying the mode of action of barley straw in cyanobacterial growth control
authors: Iredale RS, McDonald AT, Adams DG
organism: Microcystis PCC 7806 (Pasteur collection) and Microcystis SD053 (Yorkshire reservoir isolate, not axenic)
dose: Lab doses far above field rates: 40 g wet (~4 g dry) straw/L in the activation time course; fresh finely chopped straw 0.1-5 g dry/L; whole straw up to 40 g dry/L; catalase 5 mg/mL
duration: Three or more weeks of decomposition
result: Whole fresh straw (~4 g dry/L) did not inhibit Microcystis at first; inhibition rose as straw decomposed, peaking at ~1000 h, then declined, and liquor alone only cut growth to ~80% of control. Finely chopped fresh straw inhibited at 5 g dry/L at 20 °C and down to 1 g/L (PCC 7806) or above 0.1 g/L (SD053) at 27 °C, while whole fresh straw gave no inhibition even at 20 g dry/L.
key_details: Series of flask bioassays (triplicate, three no-straw controls each, 7-14 days, Chl a daily) on two Microcystis strains. Autoclaved straw in sterile dialysis packages had no effect on Microcystis SD053 over two weeks, showing microbial decomposition is needed to activate whole straw. Straw decomposed under UV-supplemented light was more inhibitory than under visible light, and daily catalase reduced inhibition, consistent with a hydrogen peroxide role. Outcome depended on temperature (stronger at 27 than 20 °C) and strain (PCC 7806 more resistant, partly recovered after ~200 h). In some bioassays only two of three replicates were inhibited.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gives no doses; the effective lab doses (grams of straw per litre) are roughly 20-100 times the ~25-50 g/m3 used in the field, which matters for any field inference.

title: Laboratory tests of ammonium and barley straw extract as agents to suppress abundance of the harmful alga Prymnesium parvum and its toxicity to fish
authors: Grover JP, Baker JW, Ureña-Boeck F, Brooks BW, Errera RM, Roelke DL, Kiesling RL
scale: Lab batch cultures, complete 5 x 3 factorial (control, low/high ammonium, low/high BSE x 10, 20, 30 °C), each combination in duplicate, plus fathead minnow (P. promelas) toxicity tests
dose: Weekly on days 0, 7, 14, 21: barley straw extract 0.015 mL/L (manufacturer's highest recommended pond dose) or 0.75 mL/L (50x); ammonium +0.4 or +40 µmol/L
result: No barley straw extract dose significantly reduced P. parvum growth, endpoint density or fish toxicity; low BSE at 30 °C raised growth rate ~10%. High ammonium (40 µmol/L weekly) cut endpoint density by about 50% and abolished fish toxicity, although it raised early exponential growth rate by 0.065 per day.
key_details: Factorial lab test (duplicates) of a commercial barley straw extract and ammonium against Prymnesium parvum at three temperatures for 23 days. Fish toxicity at day 23 appeared only in 20 °C cultures without high ammonium (LC50 4-17% culture dilution over 48 h); toxic cultures all had >6x10^5 cells/mL and pH >9.0. BSE contained phenolics but negligible nutrients. BSE also raised day-23 pH by about 0.5 units at 30 °C. Replication was only duplicate per treatment-temperature cell.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's ammonium note is incomplete: high ammonium reduced endpoint density by ~50% but increased early exponential growth rate. BSE was not just ineffective; the low dose slightly increased growth (~10%) at 30 °C.

title: Efficiency evaluation of an algistatic treatment based on barley straw in a hypertrophic pond
authors: Prygiel E, Charriau A, Descamps R, Prygiel J, Ouddane B, Billon G
venue: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
scale: Whole hypertrophic pond, Northern France (240,000 m3, mean depth 1.92 m, ~39 d flushing), five sampling stations, single treated pond with no untreated control
dose: 3 tons barley straw (50 g/m2, CEH 2004 guidance) in 150 loose rolls on five floating anchored structures with 50 buoys to keep it aerobic; added early May 2010
result: Barley straw did not prevent cyanobacteria: Aphanizomenon dominated the phytoplankton on 4 June, 17 July and 22 July 2010 (with an A. flos-aquae scum on 4 June), and Chl a ranged 8-83 ug/L. Authors judged it not appropriate for this pond type.
env_effects: Pond remained well oxygenated; no community shift observed.
key_details: Before/during monitoring of one treated pond from February to November 2010 with water and sediment chemistry at five stations; no control pond, so the design cannot separate treatment from seasonal succession. Straw dose followed the UK CEH recommendation (50 g/m2, 3 t total) and was kept floating and aerobic. Cyanobacteria (Aphanizomenon, later Aphanocapsa, Anabaena) still dominated in summer; nitrate limitation and sediment P release are discussed as drivers. Pond was well oxygenated through all seasons.
fulltext_discrepancy: Dose was missing in the record (it is the standard 50 g/m2); record should state the design lacks any untreated control.

title: The influence of active metabolites from the decomposition of camelina and barley straw on the development of phytoplankton from eutrophic freshwater ecosystem
authors: Świerk D, Celewicz-Gołdyn S, Krzyżaniak M, Antoszewski P, Stuper-Szablewska K, Szablewski T, et al.
organism: Mixed phytoplankton from a eutrophic reservoir (chrysophytes, cyanobacteria, dinoflagellates, green algae)
scale: 15 glass aquaria (5 control, 5 barley, 5 camelina) with reservoir water and sediment
dose: 20 g barley or camelina straw per aquarium
result: Camelina straw had the strongest inhibitory effect on chrysophytes, potentially toxic cyanobacteria and dinoflagellates, via polyphenols (mainly gallic and caffeic acids, flavonoids); barley straw was the comparison. Polyphenols simultaneously promoted filamentous green algae.
env_effects: Filamentous green algae stimulated; lower total molds and bacteria with straw vs control.

title: Algal growth control by a barley straw extract
authors: Ball AS, Williams M, Vincent D, Robinson JI
organism: Lake-water algae; Microcystis sp. and Scenedesmus
dose: Chopped straw 1% w/v (1 g in 200 mL lake water); extracts 1% down to 0.005% v/v (Microcystis) and 0.01% or 0.001% (Scenedesmus)
result: In lake water, controls rose ~10-fold to ~400 µg/L Chl a and wheat straw to 1160 µg/L, while no algal growth was detected with barley straw over 28 days. Decomposed-barley extract held Microcystis at 226-457 µg/L vs 3710 µg/L in controls (about 10-fold lower at every dose down to 0.005%), whereas fresh-barley extract slightly increased growth; Scenedesmus was fully inhibited at 0.01% but not at 0.001%.
env_effects: Not assessed; lignin content of straw rose from 10 to 33% during decomposition.
key_details: Flask experiments, triplicate, 20 °C, continuous light (375 µmol/m2/s), up to 28 days. Lake water (initial Chl a ~40 µg/L) with 1% chopped barley or wheat straw vs control; then Microcystis and Scenedesmus cultures in Bold's basal medium with fresh vs decomposed-barley extract. Decomposed straw had 33% lignin. Decomposed-barley extract at 1% gave 351 vs 3710 µg/L Chl a (about 91% lower); at 0.005% it gave 386 µg/L. Wheat straw stimulated algae, presumably by nutrient leaching; fresh-barley extract gave no inhibition. No field test.

title: Use of barley straw to control nuisance freshwater algae
organism: Microcystis aeruginosa, Anabaena flos-aquae, Scenedesmus, Spirogyra, Cladophora, Hydrodictyon, Oscillatoria
scale: Lab bioassays (triplicate tubes, 14 days) of seven algae plus field trial in nine 300 m2 earthen ponds (20 x 15 x 1 m) in Iran: 3 ponds at 400 kg/ha, 3 at 800 kg/ha, 3 untreated controls
dose: Lab: straw liquor from 360 g chopped straw in 18 L water rotted 60 days, 10 mL per 30 mL tube; field: 400 and 800 kg/ha straw bales
duration: Lab 14 days; ponds April-August 2008 (about four months)
result: In ponds, control Chl a rose to 1,180 µg/L after four months while both straw treatments peaked at ~460 µg/L after one month and fell to 223 (400 kg/ha) and 106 µg/L (800 kg/ha); mean total phytoplankton density was 76.51 vs 32.08 and 30.26 x10^4 units/mL, and cyanobacteria 40.99 vs 7.16 and 6.47 x10^4 units/mL. In the lab, M. aeruginosa Chl a was almost undetectable after two weeks, and Scenedesmus and Anabaena were eight and five times lower than controls.
env_effects: Nitrate-N significantly higher in treated ponds (1.65-1.72 vs 0.83 mg/L); reactive P slightly lower and dissolved oxygen not significantly different. Diatoms became dominant (>56% by August) in treated ponds while cyanobacteria stayed dominant (69%) in controls; Chrysophyceae significantly reduced. Hydrodictyon (and non-significantly Oscillatoria) stimulated in the lab.
key_details: Replicated pond trial (three ponds per treatment, randomly assigned) in problem ponds in Iran, April-August 2008, with lab bioassays of seven species in triplicate. Final Chl a was 81% (400 kg/ha) and 91% (800 kg/ha) below controls; total phytoplankton density was about 58-60% lower and cyanobacteria about 83-84% lower. The 800 kg/ha dose was not significantly better than 400 kg/ha for density. Both treatments reached ~460 µg/L Chl a after one month, so the effect built up after a lag. effect_pct 81 = final Chl a reduction at 400 kg/ha vs control.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record had no numbers or duration; full text gives a replicated pond trial (n = 3 per arm) with 81-91% lower final Chl a and a rise in nitrate in treated ponds.

title: Growth inhibition of bloom-forming cyanobacterium Microcystis aeruginosa by rice straw extract
authors: Park M-H, Han M, Ahn C-Y, Kim H-S, Yoon B-D, Oh H-M
scale: Lab flasks of M. aeruginosa in natural water from Daechung Reservoir and two field ponds (Korea), duplicate experiments
dose: Rice straw extract 0.01-10 mg/L; salicylic acid 0.1 mg/L
result: All rice straw extract doses (0.01-10 mg/L) significantly reduced M. aeruginosa cells over 8 days, and 10 mg/L gave 98% inhibition on day 8. Singly, salicylic acid at 0.1 mg/L was the best allelochemical (26%), while a mixture of p-coumaric, salicylic and benzoic acids at 0.01 mg/L gave 66% inhibition.
env_effects: Not assessed; proposed as environment-friendly biomaterial.
key_details: M. aeruginosa grown in natural waters and treated with 0.01, 0.1, 1 and 10 mg/L rice straw extract; cells counted by haemacytometer every 2 days for 8 days; experiments in duplicate. Autoclaved and filtered extracts behaved alike, and inhibition was weaker in the more nutrient-rich pond water (pond I: 630 µg/L NO3-N, 120 µg/L PO4-P) and stronger by day 7 than day 3. Several single phenolics slightly stimulated growth at one of the two doses. No field application.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits the headline 98% inhibition at 10 mg/L and the 66% inhibition of the three-phenolic mixture; replication was only duplicate.

title: Barley (Hordeum vulgare)-induced growth inhibition of algae: a review
result: Narrative review: early barley field studies lacked controls and replication and relied on visual assessment, lab results are species-dependent (inhibition, stimulation or no change) and not comparable because liquor preparation methods vary; lignin-derived phenolics are proposed as the driver. Cites field rates of 50 and later 25 g/m3 (Everall and Lees) and lab inhibition down to 1 g/m3 and 0.005% liquor.
env_effects: Cites other mechanisms: straw supplying carbon to bacteria that compete for P, and bales trapping sediment, improving clarity and allowing Elodea canadensis to replace algae.
key_details: Review in sections on early work, further research, and lignin as the driving force, with an updated table of species responses and a table of liquor preparation methods. The authors stress that early field work had no controls or replication and was based on visual assessment prone to sampler bias. They recommend documenting barley variety, lignin content through rotting, liquor preparation, and testing multiple liquor ages and extraction methods. No quantitative synthesis of effect sizes.
